reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Presents with peripheral oedema, sometimes effusions or chylous ascites, together with diarrhoea and features of malabsorption
Characteristic laboratory findings are hypoalbuminaemia, low immunoglobulins and lymphopenia caused by enteric loss of protein and lymph
Fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies and hypocalcaemia may occur because of impaired fat and lymphatic absorption
Primary disease is a congenital malformation of intestinal lymphatics, while secondary disease results from any process obstructing lymphatic drainage
Endoscopy may show scattered white villous tips or a snow-flake mucosal appearance, and biopsy shows dilated mucosal and submucosal lymphatics
Diagnosis is supported by demonstrating enteric protein loss, for example with faecal alpha-1-antitrypsin clearance
Management is a low-fat diet enriched with medium-chain triglycerides that bypass the lymphatics, with treatment of any underlying secondary cause
reference.pathophysiology: Intestinal lymphangiectasia is characterised by dilatation of the lymphatic channels of the small-bowel mucosa and submucosa, which may be a primary congenital anomaly or secondary to obstruction of lymphatic flow by cardiac disease, malignancy, infection or fibrosis. The dilated, incompetent lymphatics leak or rupture into the bowel lumen, causing loss of protein-rich lymph containing albumin, immunoglobulins and lymphocytes. This produces a protein-losing enteropathy with hypoalbuminaemia and consequent oedema, hypogammaglobulinaemia with susceptibility to infection, and lymphopenia, while impaired lymphatic transport of long-chain fats causes fat malabsorption.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of protein-losing enteropathy such as Menetrier disease
Congestive cardiac failure and constrictive pericarditis
Coeliac disease and other malabsorptive enteropathies
additionalInvestigations: Serum albumin, immunoglobulins and lymphocyte count
Faecal alpha-1-antitrypsin clearance to confirm enteric protein loss
Endoscopy with small-bowel biopsy showing dilated lymphatics
Cross-sectional imaging and capsule endoscopy to define extent and secondary causes
Assessment of fat-soluble vitamins and calcium
redFlags: Severe hypoalbuminaemia with anasarca and serous effusions
Recurrent or serious infection from immunoglobulin and lymphocyte depletion
Features suggesting an underlying malignancy or cardiac cause of secondary disease
reference.prognosis: Primary disease is usually controlled but not cured by lifelong dietary modification; secondary disease may resolve if the underlying cause is treated, and prognosis then depends largely on that condition.
pitfalls: Attributing hypoalbuminaemia to renal or hepatic causes without considering enteric protein loss
Missing patchy lymphangiectasia when only a single biopsy site is sampled
Overlooking a secondary cause such as cardiac disease or malignancy
Failing to substitute medium-chain triglycerides and monitor fat-soluble vitamins
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Institute a lifelong low-fat, high-protein diet with medium-chain triglyceride supplementation to bypass the obstructed lymphatics
Supplement fat-soluble vitamins and calcium to correct malabsorption
Treat the underlying cause in secondary disease, such as cardiac, malignant or infiltrative lymphatic obstruction
Support the protein-losing enteropathy with albumin for symptomatic hypoalbuminaemia and management of oedema and effusions
Consider a somatostatin analogue or antiplasmin agent in refractory disease and surgical resection of localised segmental involvement
Monitor albumin, immunoglobulins and lymphocyte count, with vigilance for infection given hypogammaglobulinaemia and lymphopenia
Provide dietetic and gastroenterology multidisciplinary follow-up
